title: The Leaf Pile That Stops Growing

scenes.visual: Title card 'The Leaf Pile That Stops Growing' over a side-on cartoon of one Virginia oak in autumn colours, leaves drifting down. COLOUR MAP (both films): producers GREEN (the oak), consumers ORANGE (deer, mouse, fox), decomposers PURPLE (fungus threads, bacteria dots), matter = small GOLD dots inside leaves, soil and air, energy = one YELLOW wavy arrow. The leaf pile sits inside a pale BLUE-GREY bathtub outline drawn across the forest floor. Flat cartoon style; anything not measured is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Every autumn, an oak drops its leaves onto the forest floor. New leaves land on the old ones, year after year. So why isn't the forest floor buried?
scenes.visual: Side-on cutaway: GREEN oak, a thin layer of GOLD-dotted brown leaves on the ground. Leaves keep drifting down. A ghosted, dashed stack of leaves rises taller than the oak, labelled 'if every autumn stayed? (schematic)', then fades. A question mark pops above the ground.
scenes.narration: Every autumn, an oak drops its leaves onto the forest floor. New leaves land on the old ones, year after year. So why isn't the forest floor buried?

scenes.tts: Think of the leaf pile as a bathtub. Each autumn, a new layer of leaves pours in. But the pile stays low, year after year. Something must be draining it.
scenes.visual: A pale BLUE-GREY bathtub outline draws itself around the leaf layer on the forest floor. A new leaf layer drops in; on-screen tag '+1 autumn'. A drain plug icon at the bottom of the tub pulses with a '?' beside it.
scenes.narration: Think of the leaf pile as a bathtub. Each autumn, a new layer of leaves pours in. But the pile stays low, year after year. Something must be draining it.

scenes.tts: Start with the tap. The oak is a producer. It captures energy from sunlight and stores it in sugar. It builds its leaves from carbon dioxide, water and nutrients from the soil.
scenes.caption: Start with the tap. The oak is a producer. It captures energy from sunlight and stores it in sugar. It builds its leaves from carbon dioxide (CO2), water and nutrients from the soil.
scenes.visual: The oak glows GREEN; label 'producer = the tap'. A YELLOW wavy arrow comes in from a sun at top left and touches the leaves. GOLD dots flow into the leaves from the air (label 'carbon dioxide'), and up through the roots (labels 'water', 'nutrients'). A tap icon appears on the tub rim above the oak.
scenes.narration: Start with the tap. The oak is a producer. It captures energy from sunlight and stores it in sugar. It builds its leaves from carbon dioxide (CO2), water and nutrients from the soil.

scenes.tts: A deer eats acorns. It eats a producer, so it is a first-order consumer. A mouse eats seeds, and a fox eats the mouse. That makes the fox a second-order consumer.
scenes.visual: An ORANGE deer walks in and nibbles acorns; label 'first-order consumer'. GOLD dots move from acorns into the deer. An ORANGE mouse eats seeds, then an ORANGE fox catches it; label 'second-order consumer'. GOLD dots hop from seed to mouse to fox.
scenes.narration: A deer eats acorns. It eats a producer, so it is a first-order consumer. A mouse eats seeds, and a fox eats the mouse. That makes the fox a second-order consumer.

scenes.tts: Consumers carry some matter along from the tap toward the drain. But sooner or later, every animal dies too. Its body joins the dead leaves in the pile.
scenes.visual: Arrows of GOLD dots run from oak to deer and from mouse to fox, curving down toward the tub. A small cartoon dead mouse (simple outline, eyes as X, not graphic) lies on the leaf pile, inside the tub outline.
scenes.narration: Consumers carry some matter along from the tap toward the drain. But sooner or later, every animal dies too. Its body joins the dead leaves in the pile.

scenes.tts: Now look down into the pile. Fungus threads spread through the dead leaves. Bacteria, far too small to see, work beside them. These are decomposers. They break down dead plants, dead animals and wastes. A fungus has no mouth. It releases chemicals that break the leaf down outside its body. Then it takes in the small pieces.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the leaf pile. PURPLE threads branch through dark, holey leaves; tiny PURPLE dots labelled 'bacteria (enlarged, schematic)'. Label 'decomposers = the drain'. Close-up circle: one PURPLE thread tip releases small PURPLE sparks onto the leaf; the leaf edge crumbles into bits that slide into the thread. The drain plug icon at the tub's base turns PURPLE and opens.
scenes.narration: Now look down into the pile. Fungus threads spread through the dead leaves. Bacteria, far too small to see, work beside them. These are decomposers. They break down dead plants, dead animals and wastes. A fungus has no mouth. It releases chemicals that break the leaf down outside its body. Then it takes in the small pieces.

scenes.tts: Here is a puzzle. In one forest study, fallen leaves lost close to half their mass in a year. When decomposers use a leaf, where does much of it end up? Into the soil, or into the air?
scenes.visual: One leaf on a balance; the readout steps down from '100%' to about '55–60% left', with the caption 'about 1 year (Weimer Run leaf bags)'. A small tag under the balance: 'a balance shows how much, not where'. Two arrows appear, one pointing down 'soil?', one pointing up 'air?'. Pause card with the question.
scenes.narration: Here is a puzzle. In one forest study, fallen leaves lost close to half their mass in a year. When decomposers use a leaf, where does much of it end up? Into the soil, or into the air?

scenes.visual: Pause card: 'Into the soil, or into the air? Decide.' A 5-second ring timer counts down. The two arrows blink.

scenes.tts: Much of it goes into the air. Decomposers use the leaf as food. Like you, they release its energy by respiration. That gives off carbon dioxide and water. Some matter stays in their bodies, and rain washes some into the soil.
scenes.caption: Much of it goes into the air. Decomposers use the leaf as food. Like you, they release its energy by respiration. That gives off carbon dioxide (CO2) and water. Some matter stays in their bodies, and rain washes some into the soil.
scenes.visual: The 'air?' arrow lights up. From the PURPLE threads, a thick stream of GOLD dots rises out of the tub into the air, labelled 'carbon dioxide and water (respiration)'. A few GOLD dots stay inside the PURPLE threads, and a few trickle down with raindrops into the soil. The leaf shrinks and gets holes as the dots leave. Small tag: 'general process, not measured in the bags'.
scenes.narration: Much of it goes into the air. Decomposers use the leaf as food. Like you, they release its energy by respiration. That gives off carbon dioxide (CO2) and water. Some matter stays in their bodies, and rain washes some into the soil.

scenes.tts: A smaller part matters a lot. Nutrients, such as nitrogen, go into the soil. The oak's roots take them up and build new leaves. The matter has gone all the way around.
scenes.visual: A thin second stream of GOLD dots sinks from the pile into the soil, labelled 'nutrients'. The roots pull them up the trunk to new spring leaves. A loop arrow traces oak, leaves, pile, soil, roots, oak. On-screen: 'matter goes around'.
scenes.narration: A smaller part matters a lot. Nutrients, such as nitrogen, go into the soil. The oak's roots take them up and build new leaves. The matter has gone all the way around.

scenes.tts: Energy does something different. It comes in as sunlight. Every living thing here gives some of it off as heat. Energy does not go around.
scenes.visual: The YELLOW wavy arrow enters from the sun into the oak, then the deer and fox and decomposers each give off small YELLOW wavy arrows labelled 'heat' that drift off screen. The arrow never loops back. On-screen: 'energy: in as light, out as heat'.
scenes.narration: Energy does something different. It comes in as sunlight. Every living thing here gives some of it off as heat. Energy does not go around.

scenes.tts: Now watch the pile in a simple model. The same leaf fall comes each autumn. Decomposers drain the same share of the pile each year. The pile grows until the drain takes out as much as falls in. Then it stops growing. A real forest floor levels off only when it reaches that balance.
scenes.visual: Time-lapse inside the tub, labelled 'simple model (schematic)'. A level gauge on the tub's side reads the pile. Each autumn '+1 autumn' adds a layer; through the year the pile sinks as GOLD dots drain out. The peaks rise for a few autumns, then sit at the same height. Gauge label 'levels off when drain = leaf fall (schematic)'. No numbers.
scenes.narration: Now watch the pile in a simple model. The same leaf fall comes each autumn. Decomposers drain the same share of the pile each year. The pile grows until the drain takes out as much as falls in. Then it stops growing. A real forest floor levels off only when it reaches that balance.

scenes.tts: Producers fill the pile. Consumers carry matter along. Decomposers drain the leaf pile, so the matter goes around again.
scenes.visual: Whole picture at once: tap (GREEN oak), ORANGE animals along the side, PURPLE drain, GOLD loop arrow circling. The three words 'fill', 'carry', 'drain' appear beside each group.
scenes.narration: Producers fill the pile. Consumers carry matter along. Decomposers drain the leaf pile, so the matter goes around again.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. Line: 'Decomposers drain the leaf pile, so the matter goes around again.'
